newsitem.title: USA: GM plant in Indiana hit by UAW strike.
newsitem.headline: GM plant in Indiana hit by UAW strike.

text.p: A General Motors Corp. pickup truck plant in Fort Wayne, Ind., was hit by a United Auto Workers strike Friday, the first local contract dispute since the automaker reached a new national pact last fall.
But in a positive sign, GM said talks had recessed -- not broken off -- and were scheduled to resume at 9 a.m. EST Saturday at an unidentified site in the Fort Wayne area.

Production at the plant, where about 2,700 UAW members make full-size Chevrolet C/K and GMC Sierra regular cab pickup trucks, ended when the two sides failed to reach contract terms by the 10 a.m. strike deadline.
"We are hopeful we can get this resolved as soon as possible," said Daniel Flores, a GM spokesman.
Union officials could not be reached for comment.
Leaders at UAW Local 2209 want GM to hire more workers at the plant to cut down on overtime. The union also wants the company to address health and safety issues.
Workers at the plant produce about 1,000 units a day in two eight-hour shifts, plus overtime.
Bargainers worked late into the evening Thursday, then resumed early Friday, but could not agree on terms for a new three-year contract before the strike deadline set by the union, said Flores.

The walkout was the first strike over local contract terms since GM and the UAW reached a national agreement on a new three-year pact last November. In a sign of GM's strained labor relations, local contract negotiations have been moving slowly, and the automaker has agreements with about 60 percent of its 105 UAW locals in the United States.
That is far behind Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp.. Ford has agreements with nearly all of its 72 locals, while Chrysler has local agreements with about 130 of its 150 local union organizations.

The Fort Wayne facility is the only one of GM's light truck plants that makes just regular-cab full-size pickup trucks, which tend to be less popular than extended-cab models. But it is the sole producer of regular-cab sport side trucks.

Consumers are not likely to see any immediate shortages of pickup trucks due to the strike. GM's pickup truck sales slowed in February, which probably pushed up already-high inventories of the vehicles, analysts said.

At the end of January, GM dealers had more than a 90-day supply of C/K and Sierra pickup trucks. Complete February numbers were not available by midday Friday, but analysts said GM's total light truck inventory for February was at 107 days supply. The industry generally considers a 60-day supply to be optimum.
Analysts said GM is not likely to let the Fort Wayne situation fester because it needs UAW cooperation to pull off several key vehicle launches this year.

GM is launching 15 new cars and light truck products in 1996 and 1997, representing a quarter of its total vehicle lineup. Those products include the new Chevrolet Malibu sedan, made in Oklahoma City and Wilmington, Del., and a new line of minivans being produced at its Doraville, Ga., plant.
"These are the products that are supposed to bring GM's share back up to more reasonable levels," said Christopher Cedergren, managing director of Nextrend, an industry consulting firm.

"The last thing they want is to have any strike at a plant that has the potential of slowing their overall sales pace down," he said. "I think the union realizes that, which is why they are being rather pesky."
GM makes extended-cab and short-box versions at its plant in Oshawa, Ontario. It produces both regular- and extended-cab models in Pontiac, Mich., and heavy-duty pickup trucks in Flint, Mich.
GM's stock was up 62.5 cents at $57.625 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
